verdicts.why: In every sentence 'in quest of' is a plain searching-for, with no approval or dismissal of what is sought; any heroic flavour is register, not judgement.
Same plain 'in quest of' use; the word names the search without taking a side on it.
Tracing actions to pride or a valley to its end is neutral following-back; the sentences show no attitude in the verb.
Discovering traces of someone (traced to Clapham, traced to London) is plain detection with no judgement of the person traced.
Making a line on a surface is a physical act named plainly; no attitude is carried.
Copying a drawing through a transparent sheet is a technical process, described without judging.
Going back over a route again is neutral movement; nothing in the word approves or belittles.
Relentless pursuit is the strength of the meaning, and 'trace' itself does not carry the contempt its synset-mate 'hound' does; the sentences show plain tracking.
Travelling along a path is plain motion with no attitude toward the path or the traveller.
Reading with difficulty names an effort, not an opinion of the text or the reader.
A plan or manner that varies simply becomes different; the verb takes no side on the change.
Miss Bingley varying the music with a Scotch air is neutral diversifying; the word carries no approval of it.
'Varying circumstances' is plain dependence on a variable, with no attitude in the verb.
Being at variance with something is a factual relation; the word neither blames nor praises either side.
It names a strong negative feeling, which is its meaning, but saying someone feels abhorrence does not itself judge her or its object; strong meaning is not connotation.
Putting a footstool, a house, or a conversation into order is plainly named; the judgement in 'neatness' belongs to the sentence, not the verb.
Making arrangements for business is neutral organising with no attitude toward the business or the arranger.
Ordering the degree of importance of a request is a plain intellectual act; nothing in the verb approves or dismisses.
'Attractively' is part of the meaning, not an attitude the speaker adds; the verb itself does not take a side.
Planning and carrying out an event is described without judging the event or its organiser.
Adapting music for performance is a technical act with no attitude carried in the word.
Setting printed matter into a format is neutral craft vocabulary.
A 'spiritless condition' is a state at a time; the disapproval lives in 'spiritless', and the noun itself takes no side.
Conditions of an agreement are plain terms; the word neither favours nor resents them.
An assumption something rests on is a logical relation named without attitude.
'Condition in life' is a mode of existence; Darcy's contempt is in 'beneath my own', not in the noun.
A consideration to keep in mind is neutral; nothing in the word approves or dismisses it.
It is the plainest available name for a medical problem, unpleasant referent notwithstanding; it is chosen for taking no side, not for taking one.
The state of health in 'in condition' is a plain measure; good or bad comes from the phrase around it, not the noun.
An experimental condition is technical vocabulary with no attitude.
